To integrate RDF information into an existing knowledge base, incompatible data needs to be transformed into a compatible format. However, as the graph sizes increase, the efficiency of current integration approaches decreases due to increased processing times. Instead of updating an existing knowledge base, a new knowledge base can be created. The question remains as to how the structure of the original data should be replicated in the new knowledge base. This study proposes a novel language-oriented integration framework that allows for coherent copying of data structures, and in turn enables a predictable and scalable approach to integrating RDF information. The framework is further extended by introducing Shape Expression-based DSD and optimizing its principles to enable coherent data structure replication. Effective copying of data structures is then achieved through either instance-based or declarative copying mechanisms. The framework was evaluated on various RDF graphs, including datasets from diverse sources, and the results showed significant performance improvements, reaching three orders of magnitude better than current leading DSD approaches.

A multi-task approach using convex regression is employed to solve a financial planning problem involving multiple unknown quantities, such as a portfolio's return, risk, and asset allocation. This method's scalability is examined in detail, and its implementation in pyStoNED is optimized to handle large and small problems efficiently. A new evaluation technique known as the Assessments From Estimates method is proposed, which allows for accurate calculation of confidence intervals even in complex scenarios. R-studentization is introduced as an adaptation of a standardization technique that retains its original properties for simultaneous assessment of multiple outputs. These methods are substantiated through empirical tests presented in the paper.

To study the LHC's findings in $t \bar t \phi$ generation to determine the Higgs boson's branching ratio, the detection of the largest signals from the associated top-quark pairs with a single isolated Higgs boson must be examined. Given that these signals are extremely infrequent, combining data from the top-quark pairs with a single isolated Higgs boson and two top quarks will significantly increase the detectability of the infrequent top-quark pairs with a single isolated Higgs boson. In this context, the influence of various sub-processes on the infrequent top-quark pairs with a single isolated Higgs boson will also be investigated. Furthermore, the precision of the measured branching ratio will be estimated based on the cumulative data from the infrequent top-quark pairs with a single isolated Higgs boson and top-quark pairs.

The capability of large language models (LLMs) has been remarkably enhanced through large-scale unsupervised learning. Nevertheless, these models typically need extensive training data accompanied by precise labels in order to develop specialized skills. This research aims to unlock a new capability for LLMs - acquiring knowledge and developing skills from minimal examples without any preceding labels - thereby greatly reducing the burden of data annotation in many practical applications. To achieve this, we present a method of guided learning driven by analysis, which utilizes minimal example inputs in order to guide an LLM in generating relevant analysis outputs that provide the essential information for learning. This approach does not rely on any explicit logical frameworks or mathematical models, and during testing, it has the flexibility to select or generate analysis outputs based on the specific task at hand. In our study, we evaluated the potential of this method within the context of two critical analytical tasks - diagnosing the operational systems and identifying the intentions - and we demonstrated through our experiments that it successfully acquired the necessary knowledge from very few examples and even surpassed the performance of conventional LLMs trained with vast amounts of supervised data. This development of acquiring knowledge from minimal example inputs rather than extensive, annotated data has the potential to greatly expand the practical applications of large language models.

Automated speech identification is a rapidly growing field with diverse applications, including the investigation of historical speeches.  A key obstacle to analyzing oral histories from the past lies in processing recordings made before the digital age using analog technology.  Our research aims to expand the availability of speech identification software by developing an open-source platform that uses deep neural networks to identify German speeches.  A sizeable dataset of freely accessible German parliament recordings from the 20th century has been lacking, so we compiled a collection of randomly selected speeches from the GESIS LLaMA Corpus and used it to train our model.  Our approach successfully identifies speeches from the parliament of the Republic, Weimar Republic, and Nazi era with notable accuracy for shorter segments, also achieving promising results for longer recordings of varying ages and formats, well beyond the scope of our research.  Our software is designed to be flexible and flexible – adaptable – over time, allowing it to be used not only in academic research but also by historians, archivists, and preservation specialists in the digital humanities, along with other oral history professionals working with both modern and historical content.

Investigations into seven Be-type stars within the Large Magellanic Cloud's 30 Doradus area were conducted using VLT/UVES spectra. Four stars were identified as binary systems through their periodic wavy patterns, while the remaining three were found to exhibit distinct characteristics attributed to a possible magnetic field phenomenon, known as Be-beating-Dee. Furthermore, our analysis revealed minimal helium abundance variations among the studied Be-type stars, suggesting that their underlying physics is consistent across the sample. The study provides valuable insights into the unique behavior of Be-type stars in the Young Cluster Y* = R136, as well as possible mechanisms driving their spin-down, based on their observed properties.

We tackle the complex problem of converting noisy input text to its correct form on a large scale. To approach this, we have developed a comprehensive dataset of text pairs with various levels of noise, which we used to train a model for correcting text. However, our initial results showed that the training data itself is often flawed due to excessive noise, which causes the model to fail in real-world applications. To overcome this, we have combined data augmentation techniques to produce more reliable training data and achieved better outcomes. By applying this improved training data to the task of text correction, we have significantly enhanced the model's ability to correctly identify the correct word form in multiple languages.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and derives an optimal lower 
bound in terms of the weighted Robin Robin parameter.

Non-Exchangeable Tangent Space Embeddings (NETSE) offer a potential solution to the limitations of traditional exchangeable models, enabling more accurate representations of various types of relational data. Nevertheless, existing NETSE algorithms are either specialized or applicable to a broad range of scenarios, and often compromise on predictive accuracy or scalability. To bridge this gap, we propose a new network-based method for NETSE construction. By leveraging a Tangent Core for each node, where connections are defined by shared orthogonal matrices, we can develop a highly scalable and versatile framework. Our NTE model allows for easy adaptation to diverse network data types, including both binary and weighted networks, and we can also extend it to accommodate non-static and probabilistic scenes. Experimental results confirm that our NTE model matches or surpasses the performance of existing NETSE methods, demonstrating superior predictive accuracy and significant speed improvements, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using real-world datasets related to social networks, web graph dynamics, citation patterns, peer-to-peer networking, and neural cell communication.

In engineered quantum materials with weak interactions, our research reveals that interacting effects significantly reduce topological characteristics in non-Hermitian systems, whether periodic or disordered, by transforming topological features into degenerate features located near the gap. This reduction is attributed to the inhomogeneous broadening of spectral poles in non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and can be applied to various topological models, such as the Bi/Sm topological insulator and quantum channels. Notably, our study also shows that interacting effects preserve topological features in non-Hermitian systems for certain cases. Experimentation on quantum channels is recommended to verify the diminished topological features.

Research into the characteristics of spoken language, associated with the speaker or situation, is known as sociolinguistics. Studies have shown that aspects of spoken language, such as identity, social background and situation, affect how messages are perceived. Factors including personality, emotional state, language experience and social relationships can be identified from spoken language. This study focuses on the integration of social speaker characteristics into synthetic speech. Two experiments were conducted to assess the impact of enhancing spoken language with social speaker characteristics, as interpreted by two different models. Results showed that adding social speaker characteristics improved the perception of synthetic speech, as rated by human evaluators. However, the two models used in the study made different choices regarding which characteristics to prioritize. Improvements were seen when the speaker's identity was also varied between males and females.

A novel framework combining the modular $A_4$ symmetry and non-Abelian $U(1)_{B-L}$ global symmetry is presented. This framework successfully accounts for all observed neutrino masses and their associated oscillation characteristics. Moreover, it predicts the presence of four distinct luminous dark matter particles, which are accompanied by significant experimental indications such as a $W$ boson mass anomaly, large nuclear data inconsistencies, an observed value of $\sigma_{th}$ for scattering off nucleons that deviates from its expected standard model value, and a predicted non-relativistic relic density.

In this study, the Proton Pairing Energy is calculated using the Pairing Plus Strangeness Hamiltonian in a set of low-energy triaxial nuclei across different mass ranges. Results indicate that in most nuclei examined, the pairing energy in a deformed octupole configuration is substantial and can significantly impact the characteristics of quantum phases in a deformed potential, ultimately influencing the ground state structure. Findings also suggest that in intruder proton pairs with a collective nature, the pairing energy in a deformed octupole configuration is included within the Minimal Distance Concept and exhibits negative values, distinguishing it from normal proton pairs at the normal shape.

This paper introduces a novel class of Golay complementary structures (GCS) that can be composed of varied polyphase filter bank systems with 2N user inputs. It standardizes a multiphase filter bank's submatrix pattern across all possible orientations and orientations-invariant configurations of the GCS. By leveraging this matrix pattern standardization, it becomes feasible to construct GCS within any orientation or orientation-variant matrix size of 2N x 2N, where N is any positive integer greater than 1. Next, it is proven that a specific type of filter bank based on the GCS can be transformed into another filter bank that is orthogonal under any given orientation. As a result, it is possible to create multi-rate systems comprising two orthogonal filter banks, even in cases where the original filter banks lack orthogonality. Lastly, it is shown that a specific type of expandable GCS exists, allowing its expansion to sizes of 4N x 4N while maintaining the filter bank's orthogonality and GCS properties.

To safeguard valuable hyperspectral images from unauthorized modification, it's essential to develop a framework for detecting undetected alterations.  We're introducing EVADEC, a novel method that uses deep convolutional autoencoders to identify changes gone undetected in hyperspectral images.  Unlike traditional validation methods which rely on established feature extraction techniques or previous altered versions, our approach relies solely on the original image.  Through experimentation on various datasets, EVADEC outperformed other competing methods, achieving a notable 15% gain in detection accuracy.

Determining the remaining entropy of substances after being brought to absolute zero is a highly intricate process. This task has been undertaken in this investigation, where instead of examining real materials, we analyze model potentials and their corresponding remaining entropies. Utilizing molecular dynamics simulations, we calculate the remaining entropies of several diatomic and polyatomic molecules, which are constructed from simplified monatomic, diatomic, and polyatomic frameworks. This study found that a substantial proportion of the entropy in these systems arises from piston move and kinetic energy. Additionally, we discovered that a significant portion of the entropy in these systems is closely related to a comprehensive measure that evaluates the space with respect to configurations, which is known as configurational entropy. A semi-theoretical model was also proposed to facilitate a straightforward estimation of the entropy in these systems from their respective viscosities. Our results showed that this model is relatively accurate, specifically for polyatomics with diverse bond lengths, which further underscores the significance of entropy in understanding the behavior of complex substances.

We've developed a cosmological model based on cycling patterns similar to those seen in the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model, where cosmological cycles switch between expansion and contraction phases. Our research indicates that there's likely no need for dark energy and that its effects can be attributed to the cyclical dynamics of the universe. A mathematical model representing the universe's complex behavior is proposed, and predictions regarding the large-scale structure of the universe, the distance relationship known as D-L, and the flatness problem have been calculated. Our model also explores the possibility of a scale similar to the present horizon scale acting as an effective cycle size.

The concealed-variable framework offers a potential solution to the conspiracy problem presented in the Quantum Equations of Motion. This solution can be achieved through hidden physical variables, which must, however, comply with the constraints of the framework. One such constraint is the invariant-set requirement, which poses a question regarding how to effectively apply it - essentially, how to accurately define the set of all possible configurations within the hidden variables. Research aims to explore a superdeterministic variant of the invariant-set concept, which has the added advantage of providing a clear definition for the set of all possible configurations, thus rectifying the inherent ambiguity in the invariant-set principle. This variant is dubbed invariant-subset superdeterminism and proposed as a means to define the set of all possible configurations, which has the potential to simplify the process and provide a clear definition. This proposed version is then further refined using an example, which has the potential to provide a clear definition and offer a concrete example of how it can effectively reduce to classical mechanics, thus serving as a starting point for further research in the field.

In the future, artificial intelligence and massive, interconnected devices are expected to play a significant role in everyday life. To fully incorporate AI into our daily routines, it must be accessible not just on computers or smartphones but also within reach of everyday objects. As a result, IoT gadgets will likely become ubiquitous across various settings, encompassing common spaces, industrial environments, and agricultural operations. Consequently, a collaborative human-AI system necessitates intelligent solutions for collaborating with these devices. One crucial aspect of human-AI collaboration is communicating through everyday objects, which can be facilitated by detecting and automatically summarizing key phrases from the content of these objects. This study presents different algorithms for key phrase extraction, assesses their performance, and identifies N-Gramme as the most effective approach. This method will then be integrated into a neural network, which will be compared to other alternatives. Experiments conducted on numerous datasets indicate that the proposed solution, based on the N-Gramme model, significantly outperforms other neural networks in terms of accuracy and F1 score. This study offers a new approach for extracting key phrases from content-rich IoT data, which can be applied to various domains, including multi-knowledge domains. Furthermore, this work showcases the potential for neural networks to improve collaboration between humans and AI by enhancing the accuracy of key phrase extraction.

Using a dimer model as a precursor to a lattice QCD, we investigate the interplay of magnetic flux and dimer coverings on a square lattice. We find that in the presence of a $\pi/2$ flux, dimer configurations exhibit a natural symmetry similar to Lorentz invariance, despite this flux being non-traditional. To further challenge this idea, we introduce a Dirac fermion and an edge charge and demonstrate that these exhibit motion under magnetic flux driven by dimer movements, akin to charged particles in monolayer graphene subject to a backdoor gauge field.

Researchers have created an efficient algorithm for the sparse estimation of binary and categorical variables, and have proven its effectiveness across diverse real-world data sets. Our approach utilizes an enhanced variant of the Group-Lasso, integrated with an optimized technique commonly employed in regularization path algorithms. The latter method allows for the easy interpretation of the model's results and provides the ability to automatically select the optimal level of sparsity. Our tests on simulated and actual data have shown that the proposed method's error rates compete with or surpass those of the state-of-the-art alternative, while also being up to 100 times faster.

Ensuring the real-time performance of embedded systems is of great concern when multiple tasks are scheduled with varying priority levels and time constraints. In this study, we introduce a new hypervisor framework, designed to manage embedded systems with complex scheduling requirements, including tasks with multiple execution contexts and rapid context switching capabilities. The hypervisor framework leverages the virtualization capabilities of modern processors to provide a high-level interface for developing real-time applications. Key innovations of T-Visor, the design prototype, are the integration of real-time scheduling algorithms, including the SLF+ algorithm to optimize performance, as well as the implementation of efficient context switching and resource management mechanisms within the hypervisor. Experimental evaluations of T-Visor were conducted on a platform with ARM processors, comparing the performance of the hypervisor with and without hardware assistance. The results indicate that the integration of T-Visor with a processor provides improved scheduling efficiency and reduced overhead in embedded systems.

I introduce an innovative perspective on object perspective transformation in
low-level image processing, applying a gravitational principle to optimize
efficient image stitching. Conventional stitching methods overlook the fact
that objects in the scene are likely affected by the photographer's position.
Most existing approaches rely on the np.sync module for multithreaded image
processing, but this results in poor performance due to high overhead costs.
Diverging from standard practices, I incorporate the gravitational potential
energy in the perspective transformation formula to achieve better cosine
similarities between source and destination images. Using the OpenCV 4.1.0
library, I processed the renowned KHTech dataset at an unprecedented 35.6 FPS,
thereby identifying the optimal algorithm and demonstrating its validity with
the KHTech, Flick-KODAK, and BSRT datasets. Furthermore, I analyzed the
interdependencies between in-place data element updates and the numpy module, and
then designed a new, lightweight module with minimal global variable usage and
data element overhead costs for the gravitational potential energy.

Chimeras emerge when coupled oscillators exhibit synchronized as well as unsynchronized behaviors. Research has shown chimeras in coupled identical oscillators using the Rossler system, but not with the van der Pol model. Previous studies on chimeras used direct coupling, but it is not known if indirect coupling could support this phenomenon. Our research demonstrates the existence of chimeras in coupled van der Pol oscillators using indirect mutual inhibition in a two-population system.

Developing sophisticated controllers for today's complex cyber physical systems is a highly challenging task that involves multiple obstacles. In particular, the failure of a controller due to system disturbances or malicious cyber attacks can have disastrous consequences, underscoring the need for resilient controllers that can perform well under various circumstances. In light of these complexities, model-based heuristic approaches have emerged as a relatively simple and effective means of creating controllers, yet they are often limited in their effectiveness due to their static optimization criteria. In this study, we introduce a new model-based method that overcomes these limitations by incorporating a novel stochastic strategy for exploring different scenarios and improving system robustness. Our approach capitalizes on the dynamic capabilities of parametric linear programming to develop multiple scenarios, in contrast to the traditional static optimization methods, and also incorporates a new stochastic policy exploration algorithm that can efficiently explore different scenarios and enhance system performance in real-time. Our experimental findings validate the efficacy of this approach by comparing its performance with existing methods, including a model checkers and a previous heuristic approach.

Multi-layer graphs offer a structured representation of relationships within complex systems. Given a graph's layers that align with a group's decomposition, we can construct a dynamic system reflecting the group's operating principles. Each graph layer corresponds to a specific group, and the interactions between them illustrates the group's actions. Building upon multi-layer graphs, we introduce the concept of elevated slice algebras, derived from a specific type of graph slice that complements the graph's original structure. This leads to the establishment of a connection between elevated slice algebras and graded group algebras, as well as generalized Cayley-Hadamard algebras. This relationship enables the creation of multi-layer graphs representing elevated slices of a group's algebra, and the study of certain linear mappings within these graphs. Ultimately, we investigate the potential applications of multi-layer graphs and elevated slice algebras in dependent algebra theory, leveraging their structural interdependence as interconnected concepts.

We explore the relationship between entropy and mutual information in stochastic tensor networks by defining both concepts within the network's basis, then comparing them using the Thompson-Yoffe matrix norm. This leads us to a key observation: for a stochastic tensor network that meets certain conditions, the entropy will scale with the square of the number of network layers, and the mutual information will scale with the number of layers. This theoretical framework is applicable to other similar thermal tensor networks, and our results have implications for the thermodynamic properties of systems described using stochastic tensor networks.

Variability in individual organisms often has far-reaching implications, influencing their chances of survival and reproductive success. In many cases, the effects of this variability are modeled using mathematical frameworks that incorporate random elements. However, our statistical approach reveals that the dynamics of these models often rely on patterns in the data, which are inherited by subsequent generations. This means that the underlying patterns in the data play a significant role in predicting the probability of survival and reproductive success. Interestingly, these underlying patterns are not always apparent when looking at the data as a whole, but can be uncovered when examining the data in smaller chunks. We apply our approach to data from the Demography Simulation Consortium, which tracks population dynamics over time, and find that subtle patterns in the data significantly impact predicted outcomes.

The Hénon map, a chaotic system from the 1970s, has been widely used in various research studies, and is considered a fundamental system in chaos theory. The generalized Hénon map, with two control parameters σ and ρ, exhibits more complex dynamics and allows for multiple attractors, resulting in diverse systems with different mathematical characteristics. In this paper, we visualize the generalized Hénon map's attractors in a three-dimensional space, using different colors to represent different types of attractors, such as fixed points, period doubling, chaotic patterns and strange attractors like tori and limit cycles. This approach enables us to identify a 'chaotic region' in three-dimensional space where three types of chaotic behavior (quasi-periodic, chaotic with a dominant frequency of 1, and mixed) arise. Furthermore, we extend our previous work on systems with periodic orbits and expand our research to systems with saddle-type orbits in one dimension, and finally to systems with saddle-type orbits in two dimensions.

A solitary wave pattern emerges when the gravitational potential at Earth's surface drops due to the uneven distribution of mass.  This phenomenon can be studied through the lens of Riemannian curvature.  This work probes the connection between the solitary wave pattern and the gravitational curvature, and it reveals that a minimum amount of gravitational curvature is necessary for the solitary wave pattern to occur.  However, the pattern itself does not influence the gravitational curvature.  Furthermore, our investigation demonstrates that the conditions required for the solitary wave pattern to develop are not as stringent as those necessary for gravitational compression.

This study focuses on a specific area of $q$-analysis, exploring properties of two specialized types of partitions: those divisible by a pair and those divisible by a trio, defined as two or more consecutive integers. By developing an underlying formula, we have created tables listing the exact counts of such partitions for any set of positive integers up to a given threshold. Furthermore, we have identified the frequency distributions of the minimum hook lengths required for partitions divisible by a pair or trio. Ultimately, our research appears to be closely interconnected with a well-established concept known as "partitions with restricted differences," making a connection to the interesting area of $q$-analysis.

Investigating the Larmor tunnelion clock, a device that measures the time it takes for a spin to transition between two magnetic fields, can provide insights into tunnelion dynamics. By analyzing the oscillations of an ensemble of spin-1/2 particles transitioning between two magnetic fields, researchers found that the phase and frequency of these oscillations can be used to determine the Larmor tunnelion duration. Notably, this approach enables the simultaneous measurement of both the tunnelion amplitude and duration. In the device's current state, the results suggest a tunnelion amplitude of approximately 0.00016 keV and a duration of about 4 picoseconds, yielding a phase shift of around 0.052 radians. Furthermore, theoretical predictions based on a heavy fermion model indicate that a tunnelion amplitude of around 0.00032 keV (1 keV $\hbar$) would be required to achieve a significant, observable phase shift of about 5.8 radians. In contrast, an oscillation measurement of a spin-1/2 particle in a quantum dot would ideally yield an accuracy of about 30 femtoseconds for a single measurement, albeit with a high reliability of 95.5%.

To investigate the dominant distribution of P-wave mesons, two types – pseudoscalar and vector mesons – are examined through a nonrelativistic effective field theory.  Two types of wave functions for these mesons will be considered: minimally twisted and maximally twisted.  Analyzing the four P-wave dominants from each type as specified in the QCD factorization approach, including their quantum numbers $(J^{P}, P)$ with $(J^{P})$ values of $(0^{+}, 1^{+})$ and $(1^{+}, 2^{+})$ and P values of $0, 1, 2, 3$, reveals that the dominant distribution functions $\mathscr{T}^{(2)}$ for both minimally and maximally twisted wave functions have the same asymptotic behavior given by $(w^{2}/p_{\perp}^{2})$. However, the twist-4 distribution function $\mathscr{T}^{(4)}$ for minimally twisted wave functions has the behavior $(w^{4}/p_{\perp}^{4})$ and for maximally twisted wave functions it has the behavior $(w^{4}/p_{\perp}^{6})$. Moreover, the dominant behavior for both minimally and maximally twisted wave functions has the behavior $(w^{2}/p_{\perp}^{2})$. The twist-6 distribution functions $\mathscr{T}^{(

This study proposes a new set of nonlinear quantum operators for a Bose-Einstein condensate. Utilizing the Bogoliubov transformation, the authors derive one- and two-body Hamiltonians in terms of both physical and canonical bosonic operators. Subsequently, the grand canonical ensemble is invoked to determine the grand potential density, and key parameters such as the sound velocity and healing length are expressed solely through the chemical potential and density. Notably, the study confirms correspondence with established theories; specifically, the authors demonstrate that the Grand Canonical ensemble limit yields both Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer and Bogoliubov theories' energies. Moreover, the research shows that the effect of UV divergences can be managed by introducing a finite cutoff energy.

Recent discoveries in soft graviton physics have led to a breakthrough in understanding gravity at low-energy levels. The critical findings include the presence of Double Soft Principles applicable to both gauge and gravity theories, which Ensign et al have proven to be associated with a generalized version of BMS algebra extended with asymptical boost operators. Furthermore, research indicates that this asymptical BMS algebra characterizes the theory's spectrum of low-energy excitations. In this context, we reevaluate the role of higher-energy excitations in determining the theory's behavior at low-energy levels and revisit the theoretical foundations of EFT applications to such levels. The outcome provides an alternative perspective on recent findings in soft gravity theory and raises additional questions regarding the impact of BMS on the construction of Effective Field Theories in general.

Continuous learning is becoming a crucial component of various machine learning applications, where the challenge lies in adapting a model to ever-changing data while preserving its knowledge of previous updates. The complexity of online continuous learning lies in frequently updated data streams, unclear boundaries between new and seen data, and limited resources such as computational power, storage, and model size, restrictively limiting the number of trainable parameters. In response to these constraints, small-footprint models have gained favor, although their compactness often comes at the cost of excessive computation and limited performance compared to larger, more capable models on older data. To bridge this performance gap and integrate well-established techniques effectively, a new neural framework is proposed to combine the strengths of multiple continuous learning approaches without mimicking their constraints. The framework is called the Neural Framework for Online Collective Continual Learning (NFOCCL), an end-to-end trained, highly parameter-efficient model that can learn from multiple tasks simultaneously while being updated in real-time as the task sequence changes. The model is designed to handle collective learning challenges by integrating class activation mapping, orthogonalization, and lottery ticket hypothesis theories, making it a highly flexible framework. The framework's effectiveness is evaluated on various benchmarks, and the results show a substantial improvement in performance in terms of class activation mapping, orthogonalization, and lottery ticket hypothesis when compared to individual approaches. The proposed framework is accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/danieltlewis/NFOCCL.

In higher dimensional spaces, traditional concepts of shape and measurement are adapted and enhanced. A novel method is presented, based on a generalized approach involving the integration of four-dimensional Ricci flat metrics. This methodology is illustrated with a selection of notable examples, including the hyperboloid and hyperplane shapes, specifically in four-dimensional Euclidean space. Additionally, this framework is used to redefine the 3D sphere and torus, as well as to reinterpret the projective 3D space and torus in a new light.

In this context, a permutation function over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ is defined as a bijection within the space, and a complete permutation function is one that applies to every element of the space. The number of permutation functions and complete permutation function over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ with specific properties is investigated, with these functions and functions identified through various matrix row operations that result in distinct rows. The study shows that the permutation functions and complete permutation functions with certain parameters meet specific conditions related to linear dependence, establish connections with the finite field's multiplicative group, and ultimately provides a lower bound for the permutation functions. The research extends previous work in this area (primarily concerning $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}}$) and provides novel results for higher degree extensions.

Identifying intestinal worms is a critical aspect of sanitation, public health, and hygiene as their infestation can cause severe health issues, reduce economic potential, and hinder personal well-being. However, manual identification methods are impractical and expensive, especially in low-income countries with limited resources. This research proposes an innovative approach to automatically classify intestinal worms via micro-picture analysis using the Contagion dataset via a comparison with yolo, emulating a real-world public health scenario where medical professionals only have a limited number of images for diagnosis. The study's method employs the Deep Belief Network, as it outperforms previous models like yolo in terms of accuracy and the effectiveness of image reduction in computational cost, showcasing promising results that demonstrate the feasibility of machine vision-based public health applications.

To assess various non-zero-sum non-cooperative investment and reinsurance pricing models, we develop a dynamic programming-based MLE approach, which can handle regime-switching diffusions modeling both sublinear and superlinear scenarios. The approach's theoretical foundation is based on an a.s. verification theorem, which enables us to determine the optimal upper and lower solutions for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The method also facilitates the calculation of the second-order derivative of the value function, thereby allowing us to establish the asymptotic normality of the parameter estimator under specific regime-switching models. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through a numerical study, which examines its performance in assessing various non-zero-sum reinsurance pricing models. Specifically, we analyzed three scenarios: (1) an investment-reinsurance model with an insurer acting as the reinsurance principal; (2) a co-op investment-reinsurance pricing model; and (3) a non-cooperative reinsurance pricing model. The results indicate that our method can accurately estimate the parameters of the model. Furthermore, the parameter estimates exhibit the expected asymptotic normality. The limiting variance was estimated in each scenario, providing valuable insights into the performance of the estimator. The approach's practical utility was also illustrated through a comparative study, which examined the relationship between the theoretical asymptotic variance and the simulation-based estimated variance. The study shows that the simulation-based variance serves as a reasonable approximation of the theoretical asymptotic variance.

This research presents a method for determining optimal vertical takeoff, vertical climb, and steady flight configuration using a stochastic dual simplex method for nonlinear programming problems. Due to processing constraints, linear programming problems are often employed, but nonlinear problems provide more realistic solutions. To this end, a nonlinear problem is defined, representing the vertical takeoff, vertical climb, and steady flight configuration in multiple dimensions. However, finding a general solution to this problem is computationally infeasible, so a genetic algorithm is used to identify a suitable approximation within set parameter constraints. This approach is exemplified in both quadrotor and F22 Raptor models.

The low-energy pion-nucleon interactions are fundamentally essential due to their dominant influence on low-energy nucleon-nucleon interactions and, consequently, on low-energy properties of heavy nuclei. However, theoretically modeling these interactions at such low energies poses significant challenges, leading to significant uncertainties. A primary goal of current research is to develop effective, low-uncertainty models of these interactions, necessitating some reliance on phenomenological approaches incorporating data from pionic atoms and nuclei. Nevertheless, it is crucial for phenomenological models to be grounded in underlying microscopical theory to ensure they can accurately describe the low-energy dynamics of the Poincare group. This article discusses current developments in phenomenological models of the pion-nucleon interaction and examines the feasibility of constructing model-independent, parametrizable formulas for Poincaré-hydrodynamical loops influenced by pion emission and absorption.

The CMS pixel prototype experiment utilizes 8-sensor pixel concepts in a 50 micrometer pixel size grid, covering an overall area of around 0.1 square centimeters. The aim is to assess the accuracy and efficiency of the CMS pixel design throughout the entire production line, starting with detector design, through mechanical assembly and finally with electronics integration and test protocols. The results of the end-to-end system tests are presented here, specifically focusing on the ability of the CMS pixel to accurately locate and identify signal hits, while also demonstrating the efficiency of the CMS pixel collision reconstruction methods.

It was discovered in these end-to-end system tests that the CMS pixel is capable of achieving average track hit efficiencies of around 95 percent. The CMS pixel also successfully demonstrated an average track accuracy of around 4.5 micrometers. The CMS pixel utility for identifying multiple collision events was also tested, with results indicating that the CMS pixel is able to efficiently identify and distinguish signal hits in multiple collision events, with an average efficiency rate of around 85 percent. The capabilities of the CMS pixel to accurately locate and identify signal hits in both single and multiple collision events were also tested, with results indicating an end-to-end system single track accuracy of around 6.3 micrometers and end-to-end system multiple track accuracy of around 10 micrometers. 

It is noteworthy that the CMS pixel design exhibits excellent thermal stability, with no significant temperature-related performance variations observed, even when the temperature is altered between

We employed a machine learning framework to classify the host galaxies of active galactic nuclei (AGN) based on their morphologies. A comprehensive dataset of AGN host galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Survey was compiled, which includes diverse intrinsic shapes and orientations. We trained a classification model on a subset of hosts with observed bulge and disk components, which can then identify the dominant feature of non-merging host galaxies with a 79% accuracy. With the framework established, we analyzed the underlying host galaxy structures using two-dimensional Gaussian fitting on bulge, disk, and total images. We then applied a machine learning model to classify these host galaxies into three categories: bulge-dominated, disk-dominated, or intermediate. A validation test showed that the model identified disk-dominated, intermediate, and bulge-dominated hosts with 77%, 60%, and 62% accuracy, respectively. The distribution of the three host galaxy types is nearly even, which is consistent with the results of a previous study. Our research introduces a new machine learning framework for classifying AGN host galaxy morphologies and demonstrates consistent results with existing studies while opening the door for further machine learning applications in astronomy.

High-energy density regions in atoms and ions are characterized by unique linear and angular momentum distribution properties that result from the inverse problem's constrained hyperbolic embedding, offering valuable insights into the physics of phase-space distributions. In this context, the Wigner distribution provides an essential link, allowing for the translation of phase-space distributions into local single-particle probability densities, which in turn reveals the short-distance properties of systems like hydrogen and helium. Specifically, when specific constraints are applied to these systems, the observed probability densities converge towards their expected SCA forms, while also providing detailed information on the order of short-distance nuclear physics calculations and the possible relativistic corrections to such calculations.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning education have led to the introduction of complex-valued neural networks (CVNN), which can learn complex concepts more effectively. Nevertheless, there is a fundamental issue regarding the co-domain equivalence of CVNN, limiting its ability to be trained. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the co-domain equivalence of CVNN, exploring both theoretical and practical implications. A novel approach to co-domain equivalence is proposed, framework-independent and theoretically proven, and can be applied to any CVNN, as demonstrated by our practical implementation. The results of our numerical simulation confirm that the co-domain equivalence can enhance the performance of CVNN.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations predict the saturation of parton densities at low-x values, leading to observable saturation phenomena across various processes, including increased cross-sectional growth in proton-proton collisions beyond a certain collision energy threshold and parton saturation patterns in deep inelastic ep scattering that manifest as geometric scaling at large Bjorken-x values. Researchers have found these predictions aligned with experimental data. This review summarizes the theoretical framework and experimental evidence supporting the saturation concept, with a particular focus on its manifestations in heavy ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC.

The abundance patterns within ancient star clusters hold significant information about the early process of star and planet formation, potentially including the creation of planets. Recent research conducted by Hartwig et al. 2020 on the chemical composition of low-metallicity star clusters in the simulation Galactics a, revealed a unique arrangement of elemental ratios, however, the source of this arrangement is unclear. We investigate this mystery using the same simulation and discover that planets surrounding early low-metallicity stars lead to a uniform pattern in the star cluster's chemical composition, mirroring the findings of Hartwig et al. When planets are assumed to form relatively early, the simulation shows that the elements within these planetary bodies are either incorporated into the star cluster or dispersed through space at a rate that reflects their atomic mass. The simulation's results confirm that planet formation is the most plausible explanation for the observed arrangement of elemental ratios in the star cluster.

As AI increasingly augments financial decision-making, the issue of trustworthy automated forecasting rises. To address this, a study utilizing a unique dataset investigated correlations between human forecasting abilities and financial literacy skills. By analyzing both human and machine learning forecasts for 187 future values across 39 datasets, the research demonstrated the utility of a novel evaluation toolkit in identifying optimal hyperparameters for ML models. Furthermore, the study revealed the importance of validating ML forecasts against human forecasts, rather than relying solely on historical data, as relationships between human forecasting accuracy and financial literacy often failed to materialize. Finally, the research demonstrated the applicability of the proposed toolkit to various social and economic domains by illustrating its potential to enhance decision-making in communities.

A new approach to quantum artificial intelligence utilizing the SQUID global model is presented, with the aim of forming a quantum framework for deep neural networks. By doing so, researchers achieve a quantum representation of deep learning concepts, enabling both classical and quantum computation of complex neural architectures. Furthermore, this method facilitates direct comparison of classical and quantum layers within a single model. With the ability to run both classical and quantum, the SQUID model bridges the gap between traditional AI and quantum computing, providing a practical application for current near-term technology to tackle challenging data sets. Initially, the effectiveness of the quantum AI approach based on the SQUID model will be evaluated for image classification tasks using near-term hardware, such as IBM Q, with plans for future development of a full-scale quantum neural network.

This paper examines a type of submanifold called the distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifold from a nearly Hermitian manifold to a nearly flat Riemannian manifold. The primary objective is to obtain the component forms of the Levi-Civita connection on this type of submanifold and to derive the Nijenhuis tensor, curvature tensor, and Ricci tensor on it, using the second form of the Webster equation.

A novel technique for detecting nuclear recoil events due to various interactions is being developed at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS). This device, called PALEOCCENE, utilizes the oscillations of a 176Hf color center laser absorption spectrometer triggered by the passage of a nucleus through the detector. Being a direct detection method, PALEOCCENE is particularly sensitive to dark matter with kinetic energies less than a few hundred keV/c^2. Currently, the prototype prototype called PROTON is measuring water massecrance and optical properties in a 30 cm high column of D2O. Future developments aim to increase the device's detection capabilities by utilizing alternative solvents for astrophysical applications and by exploring scattering laws in order to make the method competitive with other direct detection methods even when only considering binary inelastic neutron scattering processes.

Colloidal particles suspended in a fluid undergo Brownian motion, which can create complex movements in the absence of external forces. Additionally, these particles can induce flow patterns in their surrounding fluid due to their Brownian rotation, causing chemical gradients to form. Our study investigates the long-term behavior of a cluster of colloidal particles trapped in a potential well, which may spontaneously organize into either simple crystal structures or more complex cluster formations. Our observations focus on the potential for collective movements in the collective cluster formations, which are made possible by the particle interactions at the boundaries between these structures and surrounding fluid. We model a domain where the chemical potential varies based on the location, which influences particle organization and allows for sustained boundary movement. Our results demonstrate that as time passes, the collective cluster formations can transform into more complex forms that range from forming branches to complex multifractal structures. These new formations maintain a stable organization of crystal structures within them, which in turn retains and amplifies the existing chemical gradient at the boundaries, leading to an increase in Bagnold forces that are responsible for the particle flow. This behavior is consistent across different initial conditions for particle density, which aids in understanding and predicting the final organization patterns of the collective cluster formations, which can be based on either repulsive or attractive forces between particles. Lastly, these chemical field-driven particle flows can be made spatially reversible or irreversible by adjusting the particle interactions.

This research delves into the theoretical approach to a class of edge states characterized by non-integral spin and orbital quantum numbers. By establishing a generalized classification, the corresponding quantum measurements possessing SU(2) symmetry are identified, and their spectral properties are categorized based on rotational invariance. A critical finding reveals that certain metrics, such as magnetorradians and diagonal correlations, remain unaffected by rotations, thereby exhibiting a universal form. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the existence of numerous magnetorrons corresponding to distinct SU(2) quantum measurements, thereby enriching our understanding of fractional quantum Hall systems.

Detecting COVID-19 infections on a large scale is crucial for preventing and
tracting the spread of the disease within communities and preventing healthcare
systems from becoming overwhelmed.  To aid this effort, researchers are studying
how the novel SARS-CoV-2 virus spreads through populations to inform prevention
efforts.  Previous research has shown that many infectious diseases form clusters
when they spread rapidly, leading to new methods being developed for identifying
these clusters from data.  These methods, known as community-finding algorithms,
are used to detect these clusters quickly, but are often limited by special
assumptions about how the disease spreads or require complex computations. 
Alternatively, many of these algorithms can be reinterpreted as geometric
problems that can be solved more easily and efficiently.  In a breakthrough
finding, researchers have developed a new grouping method that can be applied to
any data without special assumptions about how the disease spreads, without
special mathematical requirements, and can be efficiently computed even with
large data sets.  To demonstrate the power of this method, researchers have
applied it to data from contact tracing in Germany to accurately predict the
spread of the infection and identify high-risk areas.

We examine the prospect of detecting polarization "X"-shapes in CMB maps with or without foreground contamination. The foregrounds can actually enhance the visibility of these "X"-shapes if they are matched with the lensing pattern, but can otherwise degrade the signal, regardless of the magnitude of the foregrounds, by distorting the background gradient fields. This effect can significantly reduce the success rate of polynomial-based algorithms in detecting "X"-shapes, particularly in areas with high foreground contamination. By using an iterative S/N optimization approach on the foreground-cleaned map, we can combine the advantages of both foreground separation and optimization techniques, like the quadratic estimator used in Planck, to effectively polarize the foregrounds and enhance the detection of "X"-shapes. This method has the advantage of not relying on a separate optimization process for the foregrounds and can be used with or without a foreground-cleaned map to polish the background gradient signal and improve the detection of "X"-shapes. Moreover, this method has the advantage of not introducing additional noise and can be used to create a lensing map that surpasses the S/N of the foreground-cleaned map, even if the foregrounds dominate the noise level of the map. By using the foregrounds to amplify the background gradient signal and polarize the foregrounds, it is possible to create a polarized map that goes beyond the capabilities of a foreground-cleaned map.

To effectively learn tasks in dynamic environments with Reinforcement Learning, models often need to interpret natural language instructions that incorporate external information. However, current models struggle with ambiguous goals mentioned in natural language, which leads to inadequate performance in real-world settings. To address this challenge, we introduce RML, a novel reinforcement learning framework that leverages natural language to identify and clarify task-specific objectives. Our approach utilizes a goal-emulator network that predicts achievable sub-goals for any given objective. Subsequently, an experience reward-shaping module breaks down complex objectives into more manageable sub-tasks. As a result, the agent's performance in intrinsic reward increases, incorporating only the most relevant information from the original objective. Our findings indicate that agents trained with our approach efficiently use external information to accomplish tasks. Moreover, they exhibit improved robustness to ambiguous objectives and reduce unwanted variations in goal interpretation.

To model a quantum channel accurately, one common approach uses classical channels to represent the physical processes of state transformation and measurement influences. However, precisely determining the implementing channel for a given target channel is generally complex, often requiring optimal solutions that are difficult to solve exactly. To address this issue, this paper proposes a tomography method that applies the shadow tomography technique typically used in state measurement. By transforming the quantum channel into a form suitable for classical channels, this approach achieves two main advantages. Firstly, the problem of accurately modeling a quantum channel is simplified to a less complex, exactly solvable challenge. Secondly, this method's computational requirements for convergence are substantially lower than those of traditional channel tomography, despite also being based on optimal estimates. As a result, using our shadow tomography procedure, it's possible to accurately create a quantum channel model directly from experimental data and obtain clear, understandable expressions for important channel metrics, such as entanglement production and work capabilities. Furthermore, this method's high precision also enables us to quantify the effects of environmental noise on these channel characteristics. To validate this approach, it is successfully applied to models of coupled cavity quantum systems and cosmological phenomena.

This research presents a collection of precise inequalities that relate the Cheeger parameter to specific geometric measurements such as area, perimeter, width, height, and depth for a broad range of planar convex shapes, including regular polygons, body-centered hypercubes, and general body-centered polytopes in two dimensions. These inequalities also exhibit optimal values in specific situations such as regular polygons and body-centered polygons. Furthermore, the research develops a crucial criterion for equality based on the vertical slice property. Additionally, the studied inequalities are extended to higher dimensional hypercubes and body-centered hypercubes, with analysis of equality cases provided as well.

This study investigates the application of dynamic programming and the Viterbi algorithm in optimizing the path for a micro aerial vehicle to follow, given constraints such as energy limitations and the presence of obstacles. The path optimization problem is formulated as a sequence of binary decision-making processes, where the selection of a route is dependent on the previous choices made. This framework enables the use of the Viterbi algorithm, an adaptation of the forward backward Viterbi algorithm, to efficiently compute the shortest path to achieve a desired goal within a set time frame. The proposed method is validated by comparing it with a heuristic, randomly generated paths, and a rule-based path, showing that it results in a 30% improvement in time and 20% reduction in energy consumption.

Quantum fluids in bilayer graphene, when subjected to a interlayer Coulomb interaction, exhibit qualitative changes in their phase diagrams due to the impact of fermionic excitations. This distinct feature is in sharp contrast to conventional 2D electron fluids. Our high-order renormalization group analysis has enabled the determination of an effective multiparticle interaction potential for low-energy excitations in this system. The resulting phase diagram includes an unstable Floquet theorem phase at low interactions where the system exhibits oscillations between the two layers. The existence of this multi-body instability mode has also been confirmed through explicit molecular dynamics simulations. These simulations have identified a particular symmetry associated with this multi-body instability mode. Our work provides the first rigorous theoretical evidence for the existence of this Floquet mode and related phase diagrams in this system.

The conformation of half-sandwich actinide and lanthanide fullerenol sc2TbN@C80 was studied in relation to a terahertz (THz) wave pulse-based temperature measurement system over a temperature range of 20 K to 150 K. Observations indicated that the conformation of the sample undergoes a significant change from a rigid, terahertz non-emitting state to a more fluid state that enables terahertz radiation emission and corresponds to the melting point of the 2-dimensional lattice arrangement. Furthermore, the desorption of the lanthanide and actinide-based cluster within the temperature interval was supported by THz radiation intensity measurements that showed a sharp increase. These findings provide valuable insights into the dynamic conformational changes and phase transitions of 2-dimensional actinide and lanthanide fullerenol arrays on an N/B substrate at low temperatures.

Energy efficiency is a major concern for IoT devices, and this issue is being addressed by utilizing energy-saving techniques. The adoption of lightweight cryptography is necessary to minimize energy consumption on low-energy IoT devices. This work provides an overview of applications requiring lightweight cryptography, followed by an evaluation of various lightweight authentication protocols and a comparison of existing proposals in terms of computational cost, security, and suitability for application in IoT settings.

The Ramsey series is an optimized schedule of electron manipulation that enhances the accuracy of quantum simulation by minimizing the impact of undiscovered interactions. This study presents a statistical model to further optimize the Ramsey series based on its initial outcomes, yielding a more efficient protocol with a higher sensitivity for detecting interactions, particularly those involving obscure particles like dark photons. By fine-tuning the model parameters, researchers can customize the protocol to prioritize different detection criteria, such as sensitivity, efficiency, and confidence in interaction detection, with the ultimate goal of reducing measurement time. This study's findings serve as a template for applying Bayesian analysis to customize measurement protocols in various quantum simulation experiments.

A novel network centrality measure is proposed, based on a connection between the triangle inequality and Gromov distortion. This novel measure, called Gromov importance, provides a way to quantify the overall impact of a node within a network. Unlike traditional metrics that rely on path counts, this new method takes into account the actual distances between nodes and the disparities between them, using a suitable transformation. As a result, Gromov importance is capable of assessing the importance of nodes with irregular connections, such as nodes in small worlds and those within dense, fully connected networks. Furthermore, a suite of synthetic and real-world datasets were studied to demonstrate that Gromov importance outperforms or complements existing importance metrics, providing theoretical justification and empirical support for its effectiveness.

The Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity offers an innovative approach by simplifying Einstein's Theory of General Relativity, where the 30 symmetric and traceless components of the energy-momentum tensor are equally represented. Utilizing the Wheeler-DeWitt derivative, quantum gravitational effects can be examined in this framework. The theoretical foundation of this theory is discussed, including its mathematical principles and methodology for solving equations. The potential of this theory lies in its ability to provide clear, straightforward explanations for quantum gravitational phenomena. The theory also enables the integration of static and dynamic concepts, where solutions to Einstein's equations can be viewed as temporary, time-invariant components. The ability of this theory to provide a unified description is a significant advantage. The The Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity is a first attempt to simplify General Relativity, where the field has been difficult to work with for many researchers. The theoretical framework of this theory is straightforward and easy to work with, where the gradient map can be viewed as a fundamental tool for describing space-time. The theory also offers an alternative perspective on classical gravitational fields, where the Appell-lateral derivative is a fundamental component. The incorporation of quantum gravitational effects has been implemented through the Wheeler-DeWitt derivative. The incorporation of matter fields has also been a priority in this research. The incorporation of matter fields has been a challenging task in this research, where the field of the wave function plays a crucial role. This work commences with a comprehensive overview of various classifications inherent to matrix pencil structures, encompassing both general- and restricted-format listings. The text proceeds by establishing key principles governing non-degenerate configurations of matrix pencils in relation to nonlinear parametric families. The study goes on to explore fundamental properties within the realm of non-degenerate matrix pencils, encompassing uniqueness, determinacy, and canonical representation. Importantly, this work delves into fundamental properties within the realm of general non-degenerate matrix pencils, specifically: (i) derivative pencils arising from general non-degenerate matrix pencils; (ii) general non-degenerate matrix pencils derived from 2-matching (bipartite graph) matrix pencils; (iii) characteristic matrix pencils describing control problems; and (iv) characteristic matrix pencils describing state space realizations. Additionally, this work establishes a connection between equivalences of matrix pencils and their derivative pencils. The study concludes by illustrating a wide variety of practical applications involving discrete-time dynamical system realizations, dynamical traces, and control problems within the realm of stringent equivalence.

A novel method is formulated to compute the one-forms that couple to Kaluza-Klein monopole and Hopf bundle charges, using a geometric approach. This approach develops a geometric classification for twisted torus surfaces based on a non-abelian T-duality transformation. The non-abelian T-duality charges are formulated in terms of symmetric connections and, consequently, in terms of 3-cocycles, providing a geometric structuring for the corresponding classification. The non-abelian T-duality transformation is applied to a particular example, a twisted torus surface with monopole-like properties, and the results are compared to those obtained through commutative algebra in a previous study. Furthermore, the findings suggest that certain twisted torus surfaces may support Kaluza-Klein monopole charges and, intriguingly, may represent surfaces with singularities similar to those found in vortices on the moduli space of type IIA string theory compactified on a circle.

In our research, we examine the issue of calculating short path distances in specific graph formats. We demonstrate that for graphs with a maximum degree of $d$, we can create an abstract representation with a size of $O_{d}(\log n)$ that enables computation of exact short path distances between any two points in the graph. This improves upon a previously established bound for $d=3$. We also derive an upper bound for minor-free graphs with a maximum degree of $d$, specifically $O_{d}( \log n / \log \log n)$. Additionally, we include a surprising finding that for certain types of random tree structures, the number of these abstract representations grows exponentially with a specific constant rate.

For continuous-time systems following a certain pattern, research has provided a comprehensive understanding of behavior patterns, whereas for discrete-time systems, much remains unresolved. This study tackles this mystery by identifying consistent behaviors in a specific type of discrete-time system. We establish that for a certain class of systems that adhere to certain conditions, a global pattern of periodicity can be derived from the characteristics of the system's iterates at each point. Furthermore, a necessary condition for the occurrence of certain types of complex system behaviors in a broader context is also presented.

A new technique known as QUBIT, the Qubit-excitation-driven ADAPTative variational quantum simulator, enhances the traditional variational quantum eigensolver by taking advantage of qubit excitations to take larger steps, enhance stability, and improve performance in certain situations. Taking into account that excitations facilitated by the transverse field Ising model have a relatively low energy spectrum and grow exponentially slow, QUBIT employs a critical point to switch from iterative to adaptive approaches based on energy calculations. Previously, researchers had relied on relying solely on expectation values or approximating the lowest excitation energies directly, which can be both inefficient and computationally demanding. By leveraging the Trotter approximation, QUBIT approximates the excitation operator and uses a combination of quantum circuit Hamiltonian learning and adjoint-based gradient descent to simulate the desired Hamiltonian. When testing this method on a quantum circuit Hamiltonian of up to five qubits, researchers found that their adaptive approach performed similarly or better in comparison to traditional variational quantum eigensolver methods and achieved significantly better results in terms of convergence rate and precision. This method has the potential to bring the variational quantum eigensolver closer to widespread practical use.

In deep generative models, standard techniques for learning important data characteristics are usually separate from the actual generative process, which are then combined to generate new outputs. This paper introduces a unique approach called the profound generative decoder (PGD), an enhanced version of the standard transposed convolution (transconv) method used at the end of generative neural networks. The PDG learns a separate representation of the data and applies the maximum a posteriori (MAP) approximation to it, utilizing two interconnected stochastic units, as opposed to transconv which directly transforms an input to a desired output without understanding its internal structure. The results show that by working together, the early stages of the PDG, which represent the data, and the generative process, which produces samples, lead to highly accurate results in terms of both intra and inter class relationships, ultimately resulting in superior synthetic image quality on the MNIST dataset.

In this study, we make predictions regarding the cosmic microwave background's future accuracy and the impact of a specific model of gravitational waves generated during inflation on its measurements. The inflationary process is thought to produce a background of gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies of 10^8 - 10^10 Hz which significantly affects the background radiation. The inflationary model used in this analysis is an interesting example of a mechanism that can produce a background of gravitational waves. The predictions made in this study are based on two specific models: one that produces a certain pattern in the radiation (primordial features) and another that amplifies the existing background of gravitational waves by a factor of several thousand. The models used in this analysis are consistent with current data and predict a significant decrease in the accuracy of future measurements of the background radiation if new gravitational wave signals are detected. The impact of these gravitational waves on the background radiation is similar to the changes that would result if certain types of primordial features are present. The models used in this analysis are also found to be consistent with data from sensors that detect gravitational waves and do not yet provide any evidence for a specific type of gravitational wave known as "stochastic gravitational waves".

A recently implemented study employs the ALMA Atacama Compact Array to analyze comets, setting up observations of multiple cometary emissions in both the molecular and thermal regimes. In the course of this work, the team accidentally detected C$_2$H emissions in the course of observing CS, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of C$_2$H, CS, and CH$_3$C$O$H emissions from Comet C/2015 ER61. It's found that ER61's CN to C$_2$H ratio is similar to those of other two-tailed comets, the CS to C$_2$H ratio is distinct, and various factors influence CS to C$_2$H ratios, with location of CS emission lines and water production rates being key factors. Furthermore, it's observed that CN to C$_2$H ratios are higher in the eastern jet of ER61.
